Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit.

We represent: defendant.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a class cannot be certified under Rule 23(b)(3) where individual damages questions will overwhelm common questions.

Cite at least six decisions of the Seventh Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.
answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**I. The Class Cannot Be Certified Under Rule 23(b)(3) Because Individualized Damages Questions Overwhelm Any Common Questions.**

Rule 23(b)(3) permits certification only if "questions of law or fact common to class members predominate over any questions affecting only individual members." Fed. R. Civ. P. 23(b)(3). Predominance is demanding, and the plaintiff bears the burden of proving it by a preponderance of the evidence. *Messner v. Northshore Univ. HealthSystem*, 669 F.3d 802, 811, 815 (7th Cir. 2012). The district court must rigorously analyze the evidence and resolve factual disputes relevant to certification, even when they overlap with the merits. *Am. Honda Motor Co. v. Allen*, 600 F.3d 813, 815–16 (7th Cir. 2010). That includes testing the reliability of expert evidence on which plaintiffs rely to show that damages can be proven on a class-wide basis. *Id.*

**A. Plaintiffs must show that damages can be established through common proof.**

The Supreme Court has made clear that a damages model must measure only the damages attributable to the theory of liability on which the class proceeds. *Comcast Corp. v. Behrend*, 569 U.S. 27, 35 (2013). A model that cannot do so cannot establish that damages are susceptible to measurement across the class. *Id.* at 34–35. This Court has recognized that the mere existence of individual damages questions does not by itself defeat certification. *Butler v. Sears, Roebuck & Co.*, 727 F.3d 796, 800–01 (7th Cir. 2013). But *Butler* did not relieve plaintiffs of their burden. It addressed cases in which liability questions are genuinely common and damages can be handled through manageable procedures. *Id.* The inquiry remains whether individual issues, taken together, will consume the litigation. *See Messner*, 669 F.3d at 815–19; *Thorogood v. Sears, Roebuck & Co.*, 547 F.3d 742, 744–48 (7th Cir. 2008).

**B. Here, individualized inquiries will dominate.**

This Court has repeatedly affirmed or required denial of certification where class members' injuries and recoveries turn on facts unique to each person. In *Suchanek v. Sturm Foods, Inc.*, 764 F.3d 750, 757–60 (7th Cir. 2014), the Court held that individualized questions about what each purchaser understood, valued, and experienced defeated predominance. Likewise, *Kleen Products LLC v. International Paper Co.*, 831 F.3d 919, 925–28 (7th Cir. 2016), shows that plaintiffs cannot rely on generalized assertions of common proof. They must demonstrate that the evidence they propose will in fact resolve the contested questions for the class as a whole. *See also Parko v. Shell Oil Co.*, 739 F.3d 1083, 1085–86 (7th Cir. 2014) (emphasizing that the court must assess whether common questions truly drive the litigation, rather than assuming that a shared allegation makes the claims suitable for aggregation).

Plaintiffs' damages theory fails this test. Each class member's recovery would depend on [describe individualized facts: e.g., purchase date, price paid, use, and any offsetting benefit received], and Plaintiffs identify no method of resolving those questions with common evidence. Their proposed model [does not isolate damages attributable to the alleged violation / assumes uniform loss / relies on averages that mask variation]. That is the defect *Comcast* identified. 569 U.S. at 35–38. Determining who was harmed and by how much would require thousands of mini-trials on matters on which Defendant is entitled to present individualized defenses. *See Beaton v. SpeedyPC Software*, 907 F.3d 1018, 1025–29 (7th Cir. 2018) (affirming denial of certification where plaintiffs failed to show that class members' claims could be resolved through common proof, and where individualized inquiries remained).

**C. Bifurcation or issue certification does not cure the problem.**

Plaintiffs may suggest that the court certify liability issues and defer damages. That approach is unavailable where, as here, the same individualized facts bear on both injury and damages. When injury itself varies across the class, deferring the damages stage does not make common issues predominate. It merely postpones the individualized trials that will constitute the bulk of the case. *See Beaton*, 907 F.3d at 1029; *Messner*, 669 F.3d at 815–19. Nor does Rule 23(c)(4) permit a class to be certified on a narrow common issue simply to evade the predominance requirement. *Id.*

Because the individualized damages inquiries here will overwhelm any common questions, Plaintiffs have not carried their burden under Rule 23(b)(3). Certification should be denied or, if previously granted, reversed.
